claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, heterogeneous native oxide layer.
The native oxide layer on Q235 steel is an effective corrosion barrier at room temperature.
Protective oxide layers can hinder oxidation by acting as diffusion barriers.
Aggressive high-temperature salt exposure destabilizes the native oxide on Q235 steel.
Exposure at 700–900 °C causes a phase transformation in the native oxide on Q235 steel.
Thermal-expansion mismatch or oxide phase transformation causes oxide-scale spallation during high-temperature salt exposure.
Loss of oxide-scale continuity accelerates corrosion-related degradation.
A controlled pre-annealing treatment can form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale on Q235 steel.
The annealing-produced oxide scale will be more thermally stable than the native oxide.
Pre-annealing will reduce oxide transformation and spallation during 700–900 °C salt exposure.
Both as-received and annealed Q235 specimens will exhibit limited corrosion at room temperature.
As-received Q235 specimens will undergo significant mass loss and visible oxide spallation during 700–900 °C salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 specimens will show less mass change than as-received specimens during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed specimens will retain better oxide-scale integrity and exhibit fewer spallation events than as-received specimens.
XRD and SEM can be used to assess phase composition and microstructural condition in an annealed alloy.
Initial oxide composition and unintended surface contaminants may alter the expected corrosion behavior.
The proposed comparison controls material and exposure duration while varying pre-annealing treatment and exposure temperature.
A lack of statistically significant high-temperature improvement in annealed specimens relative to as-received controls would falsify the proposed beneficial effect of the engineered oxide scale.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says both as-received and annealed specimens should show similarly limited corrosion at room temperature, but the falsification rule says similar room-temperature performance would falsify the hypothesis.
